content: Gynecology, also spelled gynaecology, is a surgical specialty focused on the health of the female reproductive system, which includes the uterus, vagina, and ovaries. The term gynecology literally translates to the science of women outside the context of medicine. In modern practice, most gynecologists are also obstetricians, combining expertise in both fields. Historically, the ancient Greek physician Soranus, who practiced in Alexandria and later in Rome, was a prominent figure in gynecology. He was a leading representative of the Methodist school of physicians. His treatise on gynecology, which has survived through the centuries, was first published in 1838 and later in 1882, with a 6th-century Latin translation by Moschio, another physician from the same school. In the United States, J. Marion Sims is regarded as the father of American gynecology. Other notable practitioners include Dr. Benjamin B. Weinstein of Tulane University, who specialized in fertility studies. Gynecology is generally considered a consultant specialty. In some countries, women must first consult a general practitioner (GP) or family practitioner (FP) before being referred to a gynecologist. If the condition requires specialized training, surgical techniques, or equipment beyond the scope of the GP, the patient is referred to a gynecologist. However, in the United States, laws and many health insurance plans allow gynecologists to provide primary care in addition to their specialty services. This enables some women to directly consult a gynecologist without a referral. As in all areas of medicine, the primary tools for diagnosis in gynecology are a thorough clinical history and physical examination. Gynecological examinations are particularly intimate and require specialized instruments, such as the speculum. The speculum, made of hinged concave metal or plastic blades, is used to retract vaginal tissues and allow examination of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus located in the upper portion of the vagina. Gynecologists typically perform a bimanual examination, where one hand is placed on the abdomen while one or two fingers are inserted into the vagina to palpate the cervix, uterus, ovaries, and bony pelvis. In some cases, a rectovaginal examination is performed to thoroughly evaluate the pelvis, especially if suspicious masses are detected. Male gynecologists often have a female chaperone, such as a nurse or medical student, present during examinations. Abdominal and/or vaginal ultrasounds may be used to confirm abnormalities identified during the bimanual examination or when indicated by the patient’s history. Gynecologists manage a variety of conditions, including cancers and precancerous diseases of the reproductive organs (ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, vagina, and vulva), urinary incontinence, amenorrhea (absence of menstrual periods), dysmenorrhea (painful menstrual periods), infertility, menorrhagia (heavy menstrual periods, often leading to hysterectomy), and pelvic organ prolapse. There is some overlap with other specialties; for example, a woman with urinary incontinence may be referred to a urologist. Therapeutic approaches in gynecology include both medical and surgical interventions, depending on the specific condition being treated. Preand post-operative medical management often involves standard drug therapies such as antibiotics, diuretics, antihypertensives, and antiemetics. Additionally, gynecologists frequently use specialized hormone-modulating therapies, such as clomiphene citrate and hormonal contraception, to address disorders of the female genital tract that respond to pituitary or gonadal signals. However, surgery remains the cornerstone of gynecological treatment. Historically, gynecologists were not always considered surgeons, a distinction that has been a source of controversy. Advances in both general surgery and gynecology have blurred these distinctions. The emergence of surgical subspecialties within gynecology, such as urogynecology and gynecological oncology, has reinforced the reputation of gynecologists as surgical practitioners. Today, gynecologists are eligible for fellowship in prestigious surgical societies, such as the American and Royal Colleges of Surgeons, and modern surgical textbooks often include chapters on gynecological surgery. Common surgical procedures performed by gynecologists include: Dilation and curettage (D&C): Removal of uterine contents for various reasons, such as incomplete miscarriage or dysfunctional uterine bleeding unresponsive to medical therapy. Hysterectomy: Surgical removal of the uterus. Oophorectomy: Surgical removal of the ovaries. Tubal ligation: A permanent method of contraception. Hysteroscopy: A procedure to examine and treat conditions within the uterus. Diagnostic laparoscopy: Used to diagnose and treat sources of pelvic and abdominal pain, most notably for definitive diagnosis of endometriosis. Exploratory laparotomy: Performed to assess the progression of benign or malignant disease or to evaluate and repair damage to pelvic organs. Surgical treatments for urinary incontinence: These may include cystoscopy and sub-urethral sling procedures. Surgical correction of pelvic organ prolapse: Includes repair of cystocele and rectocele. Appendectomy: Often performed to remove sites of painful endometriosis implantation or prophylactically during hysterectomy or Cesarean section. It may also be part of staging surgery for ovarian cancer. Cervical excision procedures (e.g., cryosurgery, LLETZ, LEEP): Removal of the cervical surface containing precancerous cells identified on Pap smear. These procedures highlight the diverse and critical role of gynecologists in managing both medical and surgical aspects of female reproductive health.
